context: A birth costs a mother some of her pay for good — the wage-rate part of the child penalty, not the hours, which the childcare and choice model already carry. Miller (2011, US, fertility-shock IV) finds each year of delay worth about 3% in wages; Kleven et al. (2019) put Denmark's long-run earnings penalty near 20%, mostly hours. Timing it against labour-market entry rather than age (Herr 2011) shows a birth *before* a career costs less than one early in it; Bach et al. (2025, Danish siblings) find student mothers who finish catch up or overtake by 40 from university colleges, not quite from universities. Picchio et al. (2021, Italy) find the cost smallest when a first child comes 7-9 years after leaving school, and Doren (2019) that timing barely matters for the less educated. So: a modest penalty, a partial saving for a birth before a career, and the model measures both against today's timing, not against zero.
